area.name: Money and taxes
area.blurb: Paychecks, budgets, bank accounts, interest, credit, taxes, scams, and insurance, with the math behind each one.
area.intro: Money skills are life skills, and most of them come down to a little math and a few good habits. These guides cover reading a paycheck, budgeting, banking, interest, credit, filing taxes, spotting scams, and insurance. They follow U.S. rules and official sources like the IRS, CFPB, FTC, and FDIC. They teach how money works and are not personal financial advice.

guides.name: Read a Paycheck
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 10, help from about 13, do it alone from about 15.
guides.intro: A pay stub shows what you earned, what was taken out, and what you actually take home. Reading one helps you catch mistakes, plan your spending, and see where tax money comes from. The rules here are U.S. federal rules; state rules vary.
need: A recent pay stub (or the sample numbers in this guide)
A calculator
Pencil and paper
Form W-4, when you start a new job

steps.how: Look for the dates the paycheck covers and the pay date. Your employer sets the pay schedule, such as every week or every two weeks.
Gross pay is everything you earned before anything is taken out. If you're paid by the hour, it's your hours times your hourly rate, plus any overtime.
This is federal income tax your employer holds back from each check and sends to the IRS for you. The amount depends on your pay and the Form W-4 you filled out.

Together these are called FICA. Social Security is 6.2% and Medicare is 1.45% of the wages they apply to. Multiply your gross pay by each rate and compare with your stub. Your employer pays a matching amount that doesn't come out of your pay.
Many stubs show state income tax withheld. Some states have no income tax, so this line may be missing. Rules differ from state to state.
These can include health insurance and retirement plan contributions. Some, like 401(k) contributions, are taken out before income tax withholding is figured, which lowers your taxable pay.

steps.t: Check that the math adds up
steps.how: Add up every deduction and subtract the total from gross pay. The answer should match your net pay, the amount that actually lands in your account.
YTD shows totals from the start of the year through this paycheck. It tells you how much you've earned and paid in taxes so far this year.

steps.t: Fill out Form W-4 when you start a job
steps.how: Everyone fills in Step 1 (your information) and signs Step 5. Fill in Steps 2 to 4 only if they apply to you, such as a second job or dependents. The IRS Tax Withholding Estimator can help you choose.

steps.t: Update your W-4 after big changes
steps.how: Check your withholding early each year and after changes like a second job, marriage, or a new child. Too little withheld can mean a tax bill; too much means you wait for that money until your refund.

how_it_works.subject: Math
how_it_works.title: Percentages on a pay stub
body: Social Security and Medicare are flat percentages of your pay. For 2026, Social Security is 6.2% of wages up to $184,500 for the year, and Medicare is 1.45% of all wages. An extra 0.9% Medicare tax is withheld on wages over $200,000 in a year.
To use a percent in math, change it to a decimal by dividing by 100: 6.2% becomes 0.062 and 1.45% becomes 0.0145. Then multiply by gross pay.

Worked example with made-up round numbers: gross pay is $1,000. Social Security is $1,000 × 0.062 = $62.00. Medicare is $1,000 × 0.0145 = $14.50. Say the stub also shows $60.00 of federal income tax and $30.00 of state tax. Total deductions are $62.00 + $14.50 + $60.00 + $30.00 = $166.50. Net pay is $1,000 − $166.50 = $833.50.
Federal income tax isn't one flat percent. It depends on your W-4, how often you're paid, and the tax brackets, so the example simply reads it off the stub.
how_it_works.formula: Social Security = gross pay × 0.062; Medicare = gross pay × 0.0145; net pay = gross pay − all deductions
how_it_works.try: Make a pretend pay stub for a $500 week of work. Figure Social Security and Medicare, make up a state tax amount, and work out net pay. Then find what percent of gross pay you kept: net ÷ gross × 100.

teach: Hand your child 10 play bills as 'gross pay,' then take some back for each tax line, so the gap between gross and net feels real.
Let your child check the FICA math on one of your own pay stubs (cover anything private first).
Before a first job, read Form W-4 together and talk through each step.
Talk about what payroll taxes pay for: Social Security mainly funds retirement and disability benefits, and Medicare is a federal health insurance program.
tips: Use net pay, not gross pay, when you make a budget.
Ask your employer about direct deposit. If you can, split it so part of each check goes straight into savings.
Keep your Form W-2 at tax time. It sums up your pay and the taxes taken out for the year, and it's usually what you need to file.
Review the benefits your employer offers. Some can lower your taxable income.

mistakes.problem: Planning to spend your gross pay
mistakes.fix: Plan with net pay. That's the amount you actually receive after taxes and deductions.

mistakes.problem: Claiming 'exempt' on Form W-4 when you don't qualify
mistakes.fix: For 2026 you can claim exempt only if you owed no federal income tax for 2025 and expect to owe none for 2026. To keep it for 2027, you must give your employer a new W-4 by February 16, 2027.

mistakes.problem: Not updating your W-4 after getting a second job
mistakes.fix: Two jobs can mean too little tax is withheld. Use Step 2 of the W-4 or the IRS Tax Withholding Estimator.

mistakes.problem: Never checking the numbers
mistakes.fix: Check the math each payday. Ask your employer about anything you don't understand.

guides.name: Make a Simple Budget
guides.time: about 1 hour to set up, then 10 minutes a week
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 8, help from about 10, do it alone from about 13.
guides.intro: A budget is a plan for your money: what comes in, what goes out, and what you save. It helps you notice when spending creeps up and makes room for goals and surprises.
need: Your take-home (net) pay and any other income
Receipts, a bank statement, or a banking app showing a month of spending
A notebook, spreadsheet, or the CFPB monthly budget worksheet
A calculator
A calendar for bill due dates

steps.how: Write down every source of money you get in a month. Use take-home pay, not gross pay, and include second jobs, allowances, or benefits.
Write down everything you spend, even small things. Receipts and your bank account make this easier. If a whole month feels like too much, start with one week.
Group your spending into categories like housing, utilities, groceries, transportation, phone, and eating out.
A need is something whose absence would put your health, safety, or ability to earn a living at risk. Most other things are wants. People's lists differ, and that's okay.

steps.t: Spot fixed, flexible, and occasional costs
steps.how: Fixed costs stay about the same, like rent or a phone plan. Flexible costs change, like groceries and entertainment. Occasional costs, like clothes or repairs, don't come every month.
Put each bill's due date on a calendar. If paydays and due dates don't line up, you can come up short even when the monthly totals look fine.
Decide how much to set aside for an emergency fund and your goals. Even a small amount helps. An automatic transfer from checking to savings makes it easier.
Subtract total spending and savings from total income. If the answer is positive, you have money left to save or spend. If it's negative, look at flexible spending first for cuts.
Each week or month, compare your plan with what you really spent. Update the budget when your job or spending habits change.

pro: If debt is piling up, a reputable nonprofit credit counseling program may help. The FTC notes these may be offered through credit unions, universities, military personal financial managers, and Cooperative Extension offices.

how_it_works.subject: Math
how_it_works.title: Percentages show where your money goes
body: A budget is mostly addition and subtraction: total income minus total spending tells you what's left. Percentages let you compare categories, even when your income changes from month to month.
To find what percent of your income goes to a category, divide the category total by your income and multiply by 100.

Worked example with made-up round numbers: take-home pay is $2,000 a month. Needs are rent $900, groceries $300, transportation $150, utilities $100, and phone $50, for a total of $1,500. Savings is $200. Wants are $300. Check: $1,500 + $200 + $300 = $2,000.
Needs are $1,500 ÷ $2,000 × 100 = 75%. Savings is $200 ÷ $2,000 × 100 = 10%. Wants are $300 ÷ $2,000 × 100 = 15%. The three percentages add up to 100%, which is a good way to check your work.
how_it_works.formula: percent of income = (category total ÷ total income) × 100
how_it_works.try: For two weeks, track every bit of allowance or gift money: what came in and what went out. Sort it into needs, wants, and savings, then find each group's percent of the total.

teach: Give a small, regular allowance and let your child plan how to split it between spending and saving.
Play a needs-or-wants sorting game with an old grocery receipt.
Put a few real household bill due dates on a family calendar and talk about why timing matters.
Track progress toward a savings goal on a chart and celebrate milestones along the way.
tips: Budget with net pay, not gross pay.
Plan for occasional costs, like birthdays, clothes, or car repairs, by setting aside a little each month.
Save windfalls, such as gifts or tax refunds, toward your emergency fund.
Keep your emergency fund somewhere safe and easy to reach, but not too tempting, such as a separate savings account.
Budgets are never perfect. The point is to notice when something costs more than you expected.

mistakes.problem: Forgetting small purchases
mistakes.fix: Keep a daily log for a while. Small buys add up fast.

mistakes.problem: Leaving out bills that don't come every month
mistakes.fix: List yearly and occasional costs, divide each by 12, and set that amount aside every month.

mistakes.problem: Giving up after one bad month
mistakes.fix: Revise the plan using what you actually spent, and try again next month.

mistakes.problem: No line for savings
mistakes.fix: Treat savings like a bill. Set up an automatic transfer on payday if you can.

guides.name: Open and Use a Bank Account
guides.time: about 1 hour to open; 15 minutes a month to reconcile
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 8, help from about 11, do it alone from about 16.
guides.intro: A bank or credit union account keeps your money safer than cash at home and lets you get paid by direct deposit, pay bills, and use a debit card. Knowing your real balance at all times is the skill that keeps you clear of fees.
need: A photo ID and any other papers the bank or credit union asks for (check its website or call first)
Money for your first deposit
A check register, notebook, or spreadsheet
Your monthly statement (paper or online)

steps.t: Know the two main account types
steps.how: A checking account is for everyday spending, with a debit card, ATM access, and bill paying. A savings account is for setting money aside for goals and emergencies, and it may limit how often you can take money out.

steps.t: Choose an insured bank or credit union
steps.how: Check that a bank is FDIC-insured with the FDIC's BankFind tool; credit unions are insured by the NCUA. Standard FDIC coverage is $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, for each ownership category.
Before you open the account, ask about monthly fees, minimum balance fees, ATM fees, and what happens if you spend more than you have.

A bank can't charge an overdraft fee on one-time debit card purchases or ATM withdrawals unless you opt in. If you don't opt in, those purchases are usually declined instead. Checks and automatic payments can still bring fees.
Write down each deposit, debit card purchase, ATM withdrawal, check, automatic payment, and fee. Update your balance each time.
A debit purchase may take a day or two to post, so the balance in your app can differ from what you've really spent. Go by your own running balance.

When your statement comes, check off each item that matches your register. Add any fees or purchases you missed. Then adjust the statement balance for items that haven't cleared yet and compare the two.
If something is wrong or you don't recognize a charge, tell your bank right away, and no later than 60 days after the statement date. Follow up in writing and keep a copy.
If your card is lost or stolen, call your bank right away. Reporting within 2 business days generally limits what you can lose to $50 or less.

pro: If your bank charged a debit card overdraft fee you never agreed to, you can file a complaint with the CFPB.

how_it_works.subject: Math
how_it_works.title: Running balance and reconciling
body: Your balance changes with every transaction. Each new balance is the last balance plus money in, minus money out. Keeping this running total is how you avoid spending money you don't have.

Worked example: start with $250.00. Deposit a paycheck of $833.50: $1,083.50. Buy groceries with a debit card for $46.25: $1,037.25. Take $40.00 from an ATM: $997.25. Your $50.00 phone bill auto-pays: $947.25.

Reconciling: your statement shows an ending balance of $994.25 and a $3.00 ATM fee you didn't write down. Subtract the fee in your register: $947.25 − $3.00 = $944.25. The $50.00 phone payment hadn't cleared when the statement was made, so subtract it from the statement balance: $994.25 − $50.00 = $944.25. The two numbers match, so your account balances.
how_it_works.formula: new balance = old balance + deposits − withdrawals; adjusted statement balance = statement balance − uncleared checks and withdrawals + uncleared deposits
how_it_works.try: Use play money and a paper register. One person is the bank and the other is the account holder. Make five deposits and withdrawals, keep a running balance, then compare it with the bank's record.

teach: If your bank or credit union offers a youth savings account, open one together and let your child make the deposits.
Show your child your banking app and point out pending versus posted transactions.
Let a teen keep the register for one family account for a month, then reconcile it together.
tips: Turn on balance alerts on your phone if your bank or credit union offers them.
Write down ATM fees and other fees too; they're easy to miss.
Keep savings in a separate account so it doesn't mix with everyday spending.
Deposit insurance covers checking, savings, money market deposit accounts, and CDs. It does not cover stocks, bonds, mutual funds, crypto, or what's in a safe deposit box.

mistakes.problem: Going only by the balance in the app
mistakes.fix: The app may not show pending purchases or checks yet. Keep your own running balance.

mistakes.problem: Forgetting automatic payments
mistakes.fix: Write each recurring payment in your register or on a calendar before it happens.

mistakes.problem: Never reading the monthly statement
mistakes.fix: Reconcile every month so you catch fees, errors, and fraud early.

mistakes.problem: Waiting to report a lost card
mistakes.fix: Call your bank as soon as you notice. The sooner you report, the less you can lose.

safety: Report a lost or stolen debit card right away. Telling your bank within 2 business days generally limits your loss to $50 or less.
Check your account often. Reconciling regularly helps you spot fraud or identity theft.
Keep your money in an FDIC-insured bank or an NCUA-insured credit union.

guides.name: How Interest Works
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 9, help from about 11, do it alone from about 14.
guides.intro: Interest is the price of using money. When you save, a bank pays you interest; when you borrow, you pay it. Compound interest can grow your savings over time, and it can also make credit card debt grow if you carry a balance.
need: A calculator with an exponent key (^ or x^y)
Paper and pencil
A savings account disclosure or a credit card statement, if you have one

steps.how: When you save, the bank pays you interest. When you borrow, you pay the lender. The starting amount is called the principal.
Simple interest is figured only on the principal. Compound interest is figured on the principal and on the interest already added, so it builds on itself.
Savings accounts show an annual percentage yield, or APY. It reflects the total interest paid over a year, including compounding, so use it to compare accounts.
Credit cards and loans show an annual percentage rate, or APR: the yearly cost of borrowing. It's the number to compare when you borrow.
Use A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt) to see what savings could grow to. The worked example below shows how.

steps.t: Use the Rule of 72 for a quick check
steps.how: Divide 72 by the yearly rate to estimate how many years it takes money to double. At 9%, that's about 8 years.
Credit card statements must show how long it would take, and how much it would cost in total, if you paid only the minimum each month.

steps.t: Pay the full balance when you can
steps.how: On most cards, you won't pay interest on purchases if you pay the full balance by the due date every month.

steps.t: If you carry a balance, pay more than the minimum
steps.how: Paying more each month cuts both the time it takes to pay off and the total interest you pay.

pro: If card debt is hard to manage, look on your credit card statement: it lists a toll-free number for credit counseling information.

how_it_works.subject: Math
how_it_works.title: The compound interest formula
body: In A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt), P is the starting amount, r is the yearly rate as a decimal (5% = 0.05), n is how many times a year interest is added, t is the number of years, and A is the ending amount.

Worked example: you put $1,000 in savings at 5% a year, compounded monthly (n = 12), for 10 years. A = 1,000 × (1 + 0.05/12)^120 ≈ $1,647.01. With simple interest you'd have $1,000 + ($1,000 × 0.05 × 10) = $1,500. Compounding earned about $147 more. The APY for 5% compounded monthly is (1 + 0.05/12)^12 − 1 ≈ 5.12%.

Debt compounds too, working against you. Hypothetical card: a $1,000 balance at 24% APR (2% a month) and no new purchases. Paying $25 a month takes about 82 months, almost 7 years, and costs about $1,032 in interest. Paying $100 a month takes 12 months and costs about $127 in interest. Real cards usually use a daily rate, so actual numbers differ a little.
how_it_works.try: Start with $100 at 5% a year. Year 1: $105. Year 2: $110.25. Keep going on a calculator for 10 years; you should get about $162.89. Then list simple interest ($5 a year) beside it and compare the two columns.

teach: Pay a little 'family interest' on money your child leaves in a home savings jar for a month, so they see money earn money.
Graph simple and compound growth side by side on graph paper and look for where the lines pull apart.
Find the Minimum Payment Warning box on a real credit card statement together and read it out loud.
The CFPB aims its lesson on minimum payments at ages 11 to 14, a good age to start this topic.
tips: Compare savings accounts by APY and credit offers by APR.
Money left alone longer has more time to compound, so starting early matters.
An account's plain interest rate doesn't include compounding; its APY does.

mistakes.problem: Paying only the minimum on a credit card
mistakes.fix: Pay the full balance if you can, or as much over the minimum as you can.

mistakes.problem: Putting 5 instead of 0.05 into the formula
mistakes.fix: Change percents to decimals by dividing by 100.

mistakes.problem: Mixing up time units
mistakes.fix: Use the yearly rate for r, the number of times per year interest is added for n, and years for t.

guides.name: Credit Reports and Credit Scores
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 12, help from about 15, do it alone from about 18.
guides.intro: A credit report is a record of how you've handled credit, and a credit score is a number based on that record that predicts how likely you are to repay. Lenders use them when you apply for credit, so it pays to check your reports for free and fix mistakes.
need: Internet access or a phone
Your Social Security number (enter it only at AnnualCreditReport.com)
A pen or highlighter for marking errors
Copies of any papers that prove an error

steps.t: Go to the official free site
steps.how: Type AnnualCreditReport.com into your browser yourself. You can get free reports from Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion every week. You can also order by phone at 1-877-322-8228.
Each credit bureau may have different information, so check each one.
Make sure your name, addresses, and date of birth are right.
Look at each credit card and loan. Do you recognize it? Are payments shown as on time when you paid on time?
Look for late payments, collections, or bankruptcy. Accurate negative information can generally stay for 7 years, and bankruptcy for 10.

steps.t: Dispute errors with the credit bureau
steps.how: Explain in writing what's wrong and why. Include copies (not originals) of your proof and a copy of the report with the error circled. Use the bureau's online dispute or send it by certified mail with a return receipt, and keep copies.
Also write to the company that reported the wrong information, with the same details and copies of your proof.
The bureau generally has 30 days to investigate and must send you the results in writing. Check your report afterward to be sure the error is gone.
A freeze is free and stops anyone, including you, from opening new credit in your name. Place it with all three bureaus, and lift it for a lender when you need to apply.

pro: If you find accounts you didn't open, that may be identity theft. An identity theft report from the FTC (or a police report) lets you place a free extended fraud alert that lasts 7 years.

how_it_works.subject: Economics
how_it_works.title: Why lenders care about your score
body: Lending money is a risk, because the lender might not get paid back. A credit score is a quick way to estimate that risk from your history. Many scores range from 300 to 850, but companies use different ranges, and you have more than one score.

According to the CFPB, scores look at things like how many accounts you have, how long you've had them, how close you are to your credit limits, and how often you've paid late. Paying your bills on time, every time, has the biggest effect.

One part you can calculate is credit utilization: the share of your available credit you're using. Experts cited by the CFPB suggest keeping it at no more than 30%. Example: a $300 balance on a card with a $1,000 limit is $300 ÷ $1,000 × 100 = 30%.
Applying for a lot of credit in a short time can hurt a score, because it can look like your money situation has gotten worse. Checking your own report doesn't count against you.
how_it_works.formula: credit utilization (%) = total balances ÷ total credit limits × 100
how_it_works.try: Make up two pretend credit cards with limits of $1,000 and $500. Try different balances and figure the overall utilization each time. Which combinations stay at or under 30%?

teach: Pull your own free report and walk through each section with your teen (cover account numbers first).
Parents can ask each bureau for a free credit freeze for a child under 16. It stays in place until you ask to remove it.
Explain that a score is a prediction about paying back loans, not a grade on how good a person is.
tips: Reports are free every week, so check them before you apply for credit.
A credit freeze doesn't affect your credit score.
If your report changes after a dispute, the bureau sends you a free updated copy.
If a dispute isn't settled your way, you can ask the bureau to add a statement about it to your file.

mistakes.problem: Using a look-alike website
mistakes.fix: Type AnnualCreditReport.com yourself. Many sites use 'free report' in their names or misspell the address.

mistakes.problem: Thinking that checking your report hurts your score
mistakes.fix: It doesn't. Checking your own report isn't an inquiry about new credit.

mistakes.problem: Checking only one bureau
mistakes.fix: Check all three; each can have different information.

mistakes.problem: Forgetting to lift a freeze before applying
mistakes.fix: Ask the bureau the lender uses to lift the freeze, then freeze it again afterward.

safety: Type AnnualCreditReport.com yourself. It and the credit bureaus won't email you asking for your Social Security number or account information.
A credit freeze is free. While it's in place, nobody can open a new credit account in your name, and it doesn't affect your credit score.

guides.name: File a Simple Federal Tax Return
guides.time: about 1 to 2 hours for a simple return
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 12, help from about 14, do it alone (with a parent checking) from about 16.
guides.intro: Each spring, U.S. workers file a federal tax return that settles up the income tax for the year before. If more tax was withheld from your paychecks than you owe, you get a refund; if less, you pay the difference. The figures here are for tax year 2026, the return you file in 2027.
need: Form W-2 from each employer
Any other tax forms you received, such as a Form 1099
Your Social Security number
A copy of last year's return, if you filed one
A free filing option (see the steps) or a paper Form 1040

steps.t: Check whether you need to file
steps.how: Use the IRS 'Do I need to file a tax return?' tool on IRS.gov. The answer depends on your income, filing status, age, and whether someone else can claim you as a dependent. Dependents have different rules, so teens should check.

steps.t: File even when you don't have to, if it helps
steps.how: If federal income tax was taken out of your pay, filing is how you get it back. You might also qualify for a refundable tax credit.
Collect a Form W-2 from every employer and any other tax forms you received. Keep last year's return handy if you filed one.

steps.t: Pick a free way to file
steps.how: IRS Free File offers free guided software from IRS partner companies; in the 2026 filing season it was for adjusted gross income of $89,000 or less, and each partner sets its own rules. Free File Fillable Forms are electronic IRS forms with little guidance. VITA sites offer free basic tax preparation in person. IRS Direct File was not offered in the 2026 filing season.
Your filing status affects your standard deduction and tax brackets. Most unmarried people without dependents file as Single.

On Form 1040, start with your income, then subtract the standard deduction. For tax year 2026 it's $16,100 for single filers. If someone can claim you as a dependent, yours is limited to the greater of $1,350 or your earned income plus $450.
Tax software, or the IRS tax table, applies the tax brackets to your taxable income. The example below shows how brackets work.

steps.t: Compare your tax with what was withheld
steps.how: If more was withheld than you owe, you get a refund. If less, you owe the difference.

Returns are generally due April 15, so April 15, 2027 for tax year 2026. If the date falls on a weekend or legal holiday, it moves to the next business day. Form 4868 gives you 6 more months to file, but not more time to pay.
Save a copy of your return and your W-2s in a safe place.

pro: VITA (Volunteer Income Tax Assistance) offers free basic tax preparation for people who generally make $69,000 or less, people with disabilities, and taxpayers with limited English (2026 filing season figure).
TCE (Tax Counseling for the Elderly) offers free tax help for people 60 and older.
IRS Free File's guided software is free if your adjusted gross income is under that year's limit ($89,000 or less in the 2026 filing season).

how_it_works.subject: Math
how_it_works.title: How tax brackets work
body: The U.S. uses marginal tax brackets. Your taxable income is split into layers, and each layer is taxed at its own rate. Moving into a higher bracket only changes the rate on the dollars above that line.

Tax year 2026 brackets for single filers (taxable income): 10% up to $12,400; 12% over $12,400 up to $50,400; 22% over $50,400 up to $105,700; 24% over $105,700 up to $201,775; 32% over $201,775 up to $256,225; 35% over $256,225 up to $640,600; 37% over $640,600.

Example: Jordan is single and earns $40,000 in wages in 2026. Taxable income is $40,000 − $16,100 = $23,900. Tax is 10% of the first $12,400 ($1,240) plus 12% of the next $11,500 ($1,380), for a total of $2,620.

Now Jordan gets a raise to $67,000. Taxable income is $50,900, which is $500 over the 22% line. Tax is $1,240 + 12% of $38,000 ($4,560) + 22% of $500 ($110) = $5,910. Only that last $500 is taxed at 22%; the dollars below the line are taxed just as before. (This example leaves out credits and other deductions.)
how_it_works.formula: tax = 10% × (taxable income up to $12,400) + 12% × (the part from $12,400 to $50,400) + 22% × (the part from $50,400 to $105,700) + … (tax year 2026, single)
how_it_works.try: Draw the brackets as stacked buckets. Use paper squares worth $1,000 each as 'income.' Fill the bottom bucket first, then the next. Count the squares in each bucket, multiply by that bucket's rate, and add up the tax.

teach: Look at a real W-2 and Form 1040 together and match the numbers from one to the other.
Use the bucket activity to bust the myth that a raise can push all of your income into a higher bracket.
Talk about why the government withholds tax from each paycheck instead of collecting it all in April.
tips: Brackets and the standard deduction change every year for inflation. Use the figures for the tax year on your return.
If you can't file on time, file Form 4868 by the deadline and pay what you can. Interest builds on tax not paid by the original due date, and a late-payment penalty may apply.
You don't have to pay someone to file a simple return; free options exist.

mistakes.problem: Thinking a higher bracket taxes all your income at the higher rate
mistakes.fix: Only the dollars above each bracket line get that bracket's rate.

mistakes.problem: Skipping a return when tax was withheld
mistakes.fix: Even if you're not required to file, filing may get your withheld tax back.

mistakes.problem: Assuming an extension gives you more time to pay
mistakes.fix: It doesn't. Pay what you owe by the original due date to limit interest and penalties.

mistakes.problem: Using the full standard deduction when a parent can claim you
mistakes.fix: Dependents use a different, often smaller standard deduction. The IRS tool and tax software handle this if you answer the dependent question correctly.

guides.name: Spot and Avoid Scams
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 8, help from about 10, do it alone from about 13.
guides.intro: Scammers pretend to be people or groups you trust, then rush you into paying or sharing private information. Knowing the warning signs, and knowing that real government agencies never demand gift cards or crypto, protects you and your family.
need: Your phone, email, and social media accounts
A trusted adult or friend to talk to
ReportFraud.ftc.gov saved in your bookmarks

steps.how: Scammers pretend to be from a group you know, say there's a problem or a prize, pressure you to act right now, and tell you to pay in a specific way.
No government agency will demand that you wire money or pay with gift cards, cryptocurrency, or a payment app. The IRS generally contacts people by mail, and it won't threaten to have you arrested.

steps.t: Treat payment demands as a stop sign
steps.how: If someone says you can pay only by gift card, wire transfer, bank transfer, crypto, or a payment app, it's probably a scam.

steps.t: Don't trust caller ID or links
steps.how: Caller ID can be faked. Don't click links or open attachments in messages you didn't expect.

steps.t: Hang up and check for yourself
steps.how: Contact the company or agency using a phone number or website you look up yourself. For the IRS, check your online account or call 800-829-1040.

steps.t: Slow down and talk to someone
steps.how: Honest businesses give you time to decide. Anyone who tells you to keep it secret is a red flag. Talk to someone you trust before you act.
Don't give your Social Security number, passwords, or account numbers to anyone who contacted you out of the blue.
Contact the company you used to pay (your bank, card company, gift card company, or wire service) right away. Report the fraud and ask if the payment can be stopped or reversed.
Go to IdentityTheft.gov for steps based on what was exposed.
Tell the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. Forward scam texts to 7726 (SPAM) and phishing emails to reportphishing@apwg.org.

pro: Report scams to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov and to your state attorney general.
Report IRS impersonation scams to TIGTA (tigta.gov) and Social Security scams to the SSA Office of the Inspector General (oig.ssa.gov).
If you shared personal information, IdentityTheft.gov has steps based on what was exposed.

how_it_works.subject: Economics
how_it_works.title: Why scammers rush you and want hard-to-trace money
body: A scam only works if you pay before you think it through. That's why scammers invent a problem or a prize and then push you to act now, sometimes telling you not to hang up or to keep it secret. Time works against the scammer, so taking your time is a strong defense.

Scammers also pick how you pay. Gift cards, wire transfers, bank transfers, crypto, and payment apps make it hard to get money back once it's sent. A credit card, by contrast, comes with more protections and ways to dispute a charge.
The stakes are real. The FTC says people reported more than $4 billion in losses last year to scams paid with bank transfers and cryptocurrency alone.
how_it_works.try: Write five pretend messages: a prize text, a 'tax problem' phone script, a friendly text from a stranger asking to chat, a real store receipt email, and a real school reminder. Have your child sort them using the four signs: pretend, problem or prize, pressure, and pay a specific way.

teach: Practice saying 'I'll call you back' and hanging up. Make it a family habit.
Agree on a family rule: no one buys gift cards or sends money because of a call, text, or message without talking to a parent first.
Look at real scam texts on your phone together and point out the four signs.
Talk about scams with grandparents and friends too; everyone can be a target.
tips: Block unwanted calls and filter unwanted texts on your phone.
Turn on multi-factor authentication so a stolen password isn't enough to get into your accounts.
Set your security software and phone updates to install automatically.
Before you pay someone new, search their name with words like 'scam' or 'complaint.'
When you can, pay with a credit card; it has more protections.

mistakes.problem: Calling back the number in the message
mistakes.fix: Look up the real number yourself on the official website or your statement.

mistakes.problem: Trusting caller ID
mistakes.fix: Caller ID can be faked. Hang up and call a number you know is real.

mistakes.problem: Depositing a check from a stranger and sending part of it back
mistakes.fix: Never do this. It's a common scam.

mistakes.problem: Waiting because you feel embarrassed
mistakes.fix: Act right away. Fast action can sometimes stop or reverse a payment.

safety: No government agency will demand payment by gift card, wire transfer, cryptocurrency, or payment app.
Don't click links or open attachments in messages you didn't expect.
Don't give personal or financial information in response to a request you didn't expect.
Social Security will never threaten, scare, or pressure you to act right away, and will never ask you to keep things secret.

guides.name: Insurance Basics
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 12, help from about 15, do it alone from about 18.
guides.intro: Insurance is a deal: you pay a regular price, and the insurance company agrees to pay for certain big losses. Knowing the key words, especially premium, deductible, copay, and limit, helps you compare policies by what they really cost in a year.
need: Your state insurance department's website
Written quotes from several insurers
A calculator
A list of what you want covered

steps.how: The premium is what you pay for coverage. The deductible is the part of a loss you pay before the policy pays. A copay is a set dollar amount you pay for a medical service, such as $15 for a doctor visit. The limit is the most the policy will pay.

steps.t: Find out what your state requires
steps.how: Most states require some kind of car insurance to drive legally, but the rules vary. Your state insurance department can tell you what's required and whether your state uses a fault (tort) or no-fault system.

Liability pays for injuries and damage you cause to others. Collision pays for damage to your car from a crash. Comprehensive covers things like theft, hail, fire, and hitting an animal. Uninsured motorist coverage helps when the at-fault driver has no insurance.
State minimum liability amounts can be too low to cover you if you cause a serious crash. Higher limits often don't raise the premium much.

steps.t: Choose a deductible you could pay
steps.how: A higher deductible usually means a lower premium. Pick one you could afford to pay after a loss.
Get quotes from several insurers using the same coverages, limits, and information, and get them in writing.
Add the premium to what you'd likely pay out of pocket. A lower premium can mean higher costs when you actually need to use the insurance.
Ask about savings for things like insuring more than one car, bundling home and auto, safety devices, or a defensive driving course.

steps.t: Check the company and review each year
steps.how: Make sure the company and agent are licensed through your state insurance department. Review your options each year instead of renewing automatically.

pro: Your state insurance department can tell you your state's insurance requirements and whether an agent or company is licensed.

how_it_works.subject: Math
how_it_works.title: Comparing deductibles by total yearly cost
body: Insurance spreads risk. Many people pay premiums, and that money pays for the few who have big losses in a given year. That's why a premium reflects the losses the insurer expects.
Choosing a deductible is a trade-off: a higher deductible lowers your premium, but you pay more when you have a claim. You can compare plans by figuring the total you'd pay in a year.

Worked example with made-up numbers for car collision coverage: Plan A has a $500 deductible and a $1,200 yearly premium. Plan B has a $1,000 deductible and a $950 yearly premium. With no claims, A costs $1,200 and B costs $950. With one $3,000 claim, A costs $1,200 + $500 = $1,700 and B costs $950 + $1,000 = $1,950. With two such claims, A costs $2,200 and B costs $2,950.

Plan B saves $250 a year in premium but costs $500 more for each claim. So B comes out ahead in a year with no claims, and A comes out ahead in any year with at least one claim. Which is better depends on how likely a claim is and whether you could pay the higher deductible.
how_it_works.formula: yearly cost = premium + (deductible × number of claims), when each claim is larger than the deductible
how_it_works.try: Roll a die once for each pretend year; a 1 means you had one claim. Track the total cost of Plan A and Plan B over 10 years. Which plan cost less in your game? Play again with a claim on a 1 or a 2 and see if the answer changes.

teach: Look at your own health insurance card together and find the copays.
Let a teen sit in when you shop for car insurance and fill in a comparison table of the quotes.
Use the dice game to show that a higher deductible is a bet you might win or lose.
tips: If you have a car loan or lease, the lender may require collision coverage.
Ask each insurer how accidents and credit history could affect your rate.
Your driving record, the car you drive, where you live, and how much you drive can all affect the price of car insurance.
Short-term health plans often have lower premiums but cover less of your costs.

mistakes.problem: Picking the lowest premium without looking at the deductible
mistakes.fix: Compare the total yearly cost, including what you'd pay if you had a claim.

mistakes.problem: Choosing a deductible you couldn't actually pay
mistakes.fix: Pick a deductible you could cover from savings after a loss.

mistakes.problem: Buying only the state minimum without thinking it over
mistakes.fix: Minimum limits may be too low for a serious crash. Price out higher limits too.

mistakes.problem: Comparing quotes with different coverages
mistakes.fix: Use the same coverages, limits, and information for every quote.
